short: The way a company makes money: who it serves, what it sells, how it charges, and what it spends to deliver that.
kid: Your lemonade stand has a plan: buy lemons and sugar, make lemonade, and sell each cup for a bit more than it cost to make. That plan is how the stand earns its coins.
detail: A business model describes how a company creates value for customers and captures part of that value as profit. It covers the customer segment, the product, the way revenue is earned (one-time sale, subscription, commission, advertising or licensing), the cost structure and the assets needed to deliver it. Two firms in the same industry can run very different models: a hotel chain that owns its properties carries heavy assets and debt, while an asset-light operator earns fees for managing or franchising hotels it does not own. In India, examples range from capital-hungry telecom networks to commission-based online marketplaces. For investors, the model shapes margins, capital needs, cash-flow timing and how the business scales, so it drives valuation. A common confusion is treating the business model as the product: the same product can be sold outright, rented, bundled or given away and paid for by advertisers.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells water purifiers outright at ₹15,000 each, while XYZ Ltd rents the same purifier for ₹500 a month. A customer who keeps XYZ's purifier for three years pays ₹500 × 36 = ₹18,000, so XYZ earns more per customer over time but waits longer to recover the cost of each machine.

short: A durable advantage that protects a company's profits from competitors for many years, like a moat protecting a castle.
kid: Imagine your sandcastle has a deep ring of water around it, so nobody can knock it down. A shop with something special that others cannot copy is safe in the same way.
detail: Popularised by Warren Buffett, an economic moat is a structural advantage that lets a company earn returns on capital above its cost of capital for a long time, because rivals cannot easily compete those returns away. The main sources are intangible assets such as brands, patents and licences; switching costs; network effects; cost advantages from scale or process; and efficient scale, where a market only supports a few players. Analysts judge a moat by its width (how large the advantage is) and its durability (how long it lasts), often looking for a long record of high return on invested capital. In India, investors often point to dominant exchanges, depositories and long-established consumer brands as moat businesses. A common confusion: a hot product, rapid growth or one strong year is not a moat; the test is whether high returns survive competition.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns a 25% return on invested capital against a 12% cost of capital, and has kept that gap for ten years despite new rivals. On ₹1,000 crore of invested capital, that is ₹130 crore a year earned above the cost of capital, a sign of a moat.

short: Something that lets a company serve customers better or more cheaply than rivals, so it can win more sales or earn higher profits.
kid: If your lemonade is the tastiest on the street, or you can sell it for less because your mum grows lemons, more friends will buy from you. That special thing is your edge.
detail: A competitive advantage is any attribute that lets a firm outperform its rivals, either by charging more for something customers value more (differentiation) or by producing at lower cost (cost leadership), the two broad routes described by Michael Porter. Sources include brand, technology, patents, distribution reach, scale, location, data and talent. A sustainable competitive advantage is one rivals cannot easily copy or buy, and over time it shows up as above-average margins and returns on capital. For investors, the key question is not whether an advantage exists today but how long it will last, since profits attract imitators. A common confusion is between a competitive advantage and an economic moat: the advantage is the edge itself, while a moat describes how well protected and durable that edge is.
example: Say ABC Ltd and XYZ Ltd both sell a pack of biscuits for ₹30, but ABC's larger factories make it for ₹20 while XYZ's cost is ₹24. On 10 crore packs a year, ABC earns ₹100 crore of gross profit against XYZ's ₹60 crore, thanks to its cost advantage.

short: Obstacles that make it hard or costly for a new company to start competing in an industry.
kid: Starting a big toy factory needs lots of coins, special machines and permission from grown-ups. Because it is so hard to begin, only a few toy factories ever get started.
detail: Barriers to entry are factors that protect existing firms by making entry by newcomers difficult, slow or unprofitable. They include high upfront capital needs, economies of scale, government licences and regulation, patents, control of scarce resources or distribution, strong brands and customer switching costs. In India, telecom spectrum, banking licences and airports involve high regulatory and capital barriers, while restaurants and apparel retail have low ones. High barriers let incumbents sustain prices and margins above competitive levels; low barriers mean any profit attracts new entrants until returns fall. For investors, barriers are one of the main reasons a company's high returns can persist. A common confusion: high barriers do not guarantee profits, because the incumbents inside the walls can still compete fiercely with each other, as airlines often do.
example: Say a new telecom operator would need ₹50,000 crore for spectrum and towers before earning anything, while a new café needs about ₹25 lakh. The telecom barrier is 2,00,000 times larger, which is why there are only a handful of telecom operators but countless cafés.

short: The cost advantage a business gets as it grows, because fixed costs are spread over more units, so each unit costs less.
kid: Baking one cupcake needs a hot oven, but you can bake twelve in that same oven at once. Making more at a time makes each cupcake cheaper.
detail: Economies of scale arise when the average cost per unit falls as output rises. Internal economies come from spreading fixed costs such as plants, research, technology and advertising over more units, from bulk purchasing power, and from specialised equipment and staff. External economies arise when a whole industry clusters, as auto-component makers have around Chennai and Pune. Scale can become a moat because a smaller rival cannot match the leader's unit cost without first reaching similar volumes; in cement, steel and consumer-goods distribution it is a key driver of margins. Diseconomies of scale set a limit: beyond some size, coordination, bureaucracy and complexity push unit costs back up. A common confusion is with economies of scope, which come from producing a variety of products together rather than more of the same product.
example: Say ABC Ltd's factory has fixed costs of ₹10 crore a year and a variable cost of ₹50 per unit. At 10 lakh units, the cost per unit is ₹100 + ₹50 = ₹150; at 40 lakh units, it falls to ₹25 + ₹50 = ₹75.
formula: Average cost per unit = (Fixed costs / Units produced) + Variable cost per unit

short: Cost savings from making or selling several different products together, because they share the same resources, rather than producing each one separately.
kid: If you are already baking cookies, you can bake muffins in the same warm oven. Using one oven for two treats saves time and effort.
detail: Economies of scope exist when producing two or more products jointly costs less than producing each on its own. The savings come from shared inputs: a distribution network, a brand, a factory, a technology platform, customer data or a sales force. A consumer-goods company can push soaps, shampoos and snacks through the same trucks and retailers; a bank can sell insurance and mutual funds to existing account holders; a super-app can offer payments, shopping and bill payments on one platform. Scope economies are a common rationale for diversification, cross-selling and mergers, and they help explain why some platforms earn better margins than single-product rivals. A common confusion is with economies of scale, which come from more volume of the same product; scope is about breadth. Promised scope benefits in mergers often fail to materialise.
example: Say a company making only biscuits would spend ₹60 crore a year and one making only cakes ₹40 crore, but ABC Ltd makes both in one plant with one distribution network for ₹85 crore. It saves ₹100 crore - ₹85 crore = ₹15 crore, a degree of scope economies of about 0.18 (₹15 crore / ₹85 crore).
formula: Degree of economies of scope = [C(A) + C(B) - C(A and B)] / C(A and B), where C is the cost of producing the products separately or jointly

short: When a product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it, as with phone networks, marketplaces and social apps.
kid: A toy phone is no fun if none of your friends have one. The more friends who join, the more people you can talk to, so even more friends want to join.
detail: A network effect exists when each additional user raises the value of a product for other users. Direct network effects occur within one group, as with messaging apps or telephone networks. Indirect, or two-sided, effects link different groups: more buyers attract more sellers to a marketplace, which attracts more buyers. UPI in India shows the pattern: as more merchants accepted it, more consumers adopted it, and vice versa. Strong network effects can create winner-takes-all or winner-takes-most markets, because users gravitate to the biggest network and newcomers struggle to offer equal value. That makes them a powerful moat and a reason investors tolerate early losses in platforms. A common confusion is with economies of scale: scale lowers costs as a firm grows, while network effects raise the value customers get. The effect weakens when users can easily use several rival networks at once.
example: Metcalfe's law links a network's value to the number of possible connections between its users. A network with 10 users has 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 possible connections, while one with 100 users has 100 × 99 / 2 = 4,950. Ten times the users gives 110 times the connections, which is why the bigger network can pull ahead.
formula: Possible connections (Metcalfe's law) = n × (n - 1) / 2, where n is the number of users

short: The money, time, effort or risk a customer faces in moving from one supplier to another, which makes them more likely to stay.
kid: If all your drawings and games are saved on one tablet, moving to a new tablet is a big bother. So you keep using the old one, even if another looks nice.
detail: Switching costs are the burdens a customer bears when changing providers: exit fees and penalties, new equipment, retraining staff, migrating data, re-connecting systems, losing accumulated rewards, or simply the risk that the new option will not work. When they are high, customers are effectively locked in, which gives the incumbent pricing power, predictable recurring revenue and low churn. Enterprise software, core banking systems, payroll providers and machines that need the maker's own consumables are classic examples. Regulators sometimes cut switching costs deliberately: mobile number portability in India let users change telecom operators while keeping their number, which intensified competition. A common confusion is equating low churn with high switching costs; customers may stay simply because the product is good, a weaker protection that a better rival can erode.
example: Say a hospital pays ABC Software ₹40 lakh a year and a rival offers the same features for ₹35 lakh. If migrating data and retraining staff would cost ₹30 lakh, the hospital needs ₹30 lakh / ₹5 lakh = 6 years of savings just to break even, so it stays with ABC.

short: A company's ability to raise prices without losing many customers, so it can protect or grow profits when its own costs rise.
kid: If everyone loves your special cookies, you can ask for one more coin and friends still buy them. If plain cookies ask for more, friends just go somewhere else.
detail: Pricing power is the ability to raise prices, or quietly shrink pack sizes, without losing meaningful volume to competitors. It usually comes from a strong brand, a differentiated or essential product, few substitutes, high switching costs or a dominant market position; in economic terms, customers' demand is relatively inelastic. It matters most during inflation: firms with pricing power pass higher input costs on and keep margins steady, while commodity producers must accept whatever the market pays. Warren Buffett has described it as the most important factor in evaluating a business. In India, analysts watch whether consumer companies can take price hikes after raw-material spikes without denting volume growth. A common confusion is treating any price increase as proof of pricing power; if volumes fall sharply afterward, or rivals do not follow, the power was weaker than it looked.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells 1 crore jars of spread a year at ₹200 and raises the price 10% to ₹220. If volume dips only 2% to 98 lakh jars, revenue rises from ₹200 crore to ₹215.6 crore, a clear sign of pricing power.

short: The extra value a company earns because customers know, trust and prefer its brand over an unbranded or lesser-known equivalent.
kid: Two teddy bears look the same, but one has a name everyone loves, so children ask for it and parents pay a little more. That loved name is worth something.
detail: Brand equity is the commercial value that comes from customers' awareness of, associations with and loyalty to a brand. It shows up as the ability to charge a price premium, win shelf space and distribution, launch new products under the same name, and hold on to customers through downturns. Marketers measure it with awareness, preference and loyalty surveys; finance measures it through price premiums, margins or a valuation of the brand as an asset. Under Ind AS and IFRS, a brand built internally cannot be recognised on the balance sheet, but a brand bought in an acquisition is recorded as an intangible asset. That is one reason companies with strong home-grown brands often trade far above book value. A common confusion: brand equity is not advertising spend; heavy spending can fail to build it, and trust can be lost quickly through a quality scandal.
example: Say a branded bottle of shampoo sells for ₹250 while an equivalent unbranded bottle sells for ₹180, and both cost ₹100 to make. On 1 crore bottles a year, the brand earns an extra ₹70 crore of gross profit, one rough measure of its brand equity.

short: A shift in which customers trade up to costlier, higher-quality versions of products, and companies push pricier variants to profit from it.
kid: As you grow up, you might want the fancy chocolate bar instead of the small plain one. When lots of people start choosing the fancy kind, shops sell more of it.
detail: Premiumisation describes consumers moving up the price ladder within a category: from entry-level to mid-range smartphones, from loose tea to branded tea, from commuter motorcycles to premium bikes, from regular to craft beverages. It is driven by rising incomes, aspiration, easier credit and changing tastes, and companies respond by launching and promoting premium variants. Because premium products usually carry higher margins, a richer sales mix can lift revenue and profit even when unit volumes are flat. It has been a prominent theme in Indian consumption in recent years, with demand at the top end of categories such as cars, housing and consumer durables often outpacing the mass market. A common confusion is equating premiumisation with inflation: inflation raises the price of the same product, while premiumisation is customers choosing better, costlier products.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells 100 phones at ₹10,000 and 20 at ₹40,000, giving revenue of ₹18 lakh. If buyers trade up so it sells 80 at ₹10,000 and 40 at ₹40,000, unit volume stays at 120 but revenue rises to ₹24 lakh, a 33% jump.

short: The percentage of total sales in a market that one company captures, measured by revenue or by units sold.
kid: If ten children buy lemonade on your street and four of them buy from your stand, you get four out of every ten buyers. That is your piece of the street.
detail: Market share is a company's sales divided by the total sales of the market it competes in over the same period. It can be measured by value (revenue) or volume (units), and the two can differ sharply: a premium brand may hold a small volume share but a large value share. Rising share usually signals a stronger product, price or distribution position; losing share can be an early warning even while revenue is still growing in a booming market. Analysts track it closely in Indian sectors such as passenger cars, two-wheelers, telecom subscribers, mutual fund assets and UPI transactions. Industry concentration is often summarised from shares using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index. A common confusion: buying share with deep discounts can destroy value, and share figures depend heavily on how the market is defined.
example: Say a market for electric scooters is worth ₹20,000 crore a year and ABC Motors sells ₹3,000 crore of them. Its value market share is ₹3,000 crore / ₹20,000 crore = 15%.
formula: Market share = Company's sales / Total market sales × 100

short: The total yearly revenue a product could earn if it won every possible customer in its market, that is, a 100% market share.
kid: Imagine every child in the whole town wanted lemonade. All the cups they could buy in a summer is the most you could ever dream of selling.
detail: Total addressable market, or TAM, estimates the full revenue opportunity for a product or service if it achieved 100% share of its relevant market. It is built either top-down, from industry reports and population or income data, or bottom-up, by multiplying the number of potential customers by realistic annual spend per customer; bottom-up estimates are generally more credible. Founders and bankers use TAM in pitch decks and IPO documents to show how large a business could become, and venture investors favour big TAMs because they leave room for outsized growth. Indian startup pitches often lean on headline population figures to suggest enormous markets. A common confusion is treating TAM as achievable revenue: it ignores competition, affordability, regulation and reach. That is why it is narrowed into serviceable addressable market (SAM) and serviceable obtainable market (SOM).
example: Say a company sells accounting software to small shops for ₹6,000 a year, and there are 5 crore such shops in India. Bottom-up, its TAM is 5 crore × ₹6,000 = ₹30,000 crore a year.
formula: TAM = Number of potential customers × Average annual revenue per customer

short: The part of the total addressable market a company can actually reach with its current product, prices, sales channels and geography.
kid: All the children in town might want lemonade, but you can only walk to the kids on your own street. The kids you can reach are the ones who count.
detail: Serviceable addressable market, or SAM, narrows the total addressable market to the customers a business can realistically serve given its product features, price point, language, regulatory approvals, sales channels and geographic reach. A startup selling an English-only app in metro cities, for example, has a SAM far smaller than the national TAM. SAM is the middle layer of the TAM-SAM-SOM framework used in business plans and investor pitches: TAM shows the ceiling, SAM shows the realistic arena, and SOM shows the share the company can expect to win. Investors pay close attention to SAM because it tests whether a big TAM figure is relevant to the actual business. A common confusion is treating SAM as fixed; adding languages, price tiers, products or regions can expand it over time.
example: Say a software firm's TAM is 5 crore small shops paying ₹6,000 a year, or ₹30,000 crore. If only 1 crore of those shops are digitised and in cities it serves, its SAM is 1 crore × ₹6,000 = ₹6,000 crore, a fifth of the TAM.
formula: SAM = Number of reachable target customers × Average annual revenue per customer

short: The share of the serviceable addressable market a company can realistically win in the next few years, given competition and its resources.
kid: Even if lots of kids on your street like lemonade, other stands are selling too. The cups you can really sell this summer are your share.
detail: Serviceable obtainable market, or SOM, is the portion of the serviceable addressable market a company can realistically capture over a defined period, usually three to five years. It reflects competition, the company's sales capacity, marketing budget, brand strength, pricing and how quickly customers switch. SOM is the most grounded layer of the TAM-SAM-SOM framework and should tie directly to a startup's revenue forecast: if a plan shows revenue far above its SOM, something is inconsistent. A credible SOM is usually built bottom-up from the number of salespeople, conversion rates and expected customer wins, then checked against the market shares achieved by comparable companies. A common confusion is picking an arbitrary percentage, such as claiming the firm needs only 1% of India, which sounds modest but says nothing about how those customers will actually be won.
example: Say a software firm's SAM is ₹6,000 crore a year. If its sales team can realistically sign 5 lakh shops at ₹6,000 each within five years, its SOM is ₹300 crore, or 5% of SAM.
formula: SOM = SAM × Realistically achievable market share

short: A market where a single company is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes, so it can largely set prices.
kid: If only one shop in the whole town sold ice cream, everyone would have to buy from it. That shop could ask for more coins, and nobody could go elsewhere.
detail: A monopoly exists when one firm supplies all, or nearly all, of a market and faces no close substitutes, usually protected by high barriers to entry such as legal rights, control of an essential resource, or overwhelming scale or network effects. Rather than accepting a market price, a monopolist chooses the price and quantity that maximise its profit, typically charging more and producing less than a competitive market would. Some monopolies are natural, where one network is cheaper than several, as with power transmission or railway tracks, and these are regulated rather than broken up. In India, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) does not penalise dominance itself but acts against abuse of a dominant position, such as predatory pricing or unfair conditions. A common confusion: a firm can hold monopoly power without 100% share; regulators look at dominance and conduct.
example: Say ABC Ltd is the only supplier of a vital chemical, and buyers would purchase 10 lakh kg at ₹100 a kg in a competitive market. As a monopolist, ABC instead sells 8 lakh kg at ₹150, earning revenue of ₹12 crore instead of ₹10 crore.

short: A market dominated by just two sellers, whose decisions on price and output strongly affect each other.
kid: If only two ice-cream vans come down your street, each one watches the other. If one starts giving bigger scoops, the other has to think about doing the same.
detail: A duopoly is a special case of oligopoly in which two firms control most of a market. Each must anticipate its rival's response: classic models describe competition on quantity (Cournot) or on price (Bertrand), and real outcomes range from fierce price wars to quiet, stable pricing that keeps margins high for both. Boeing and Airbus in large passenger jets are the textbook global example. In India, analysts often describe telecom as drifting toward a duopoly given the scale of the two largest operators, and, as of 2025, two apps handled the large majority of UPI payments. Regulators watch duopolies closely for tacit collusion and for barriers that keep a third player out. A common confusion: a duopoly does not require exactly two firms to exist; smaller players can be present while two leaders dominate.
example: Say ABC Ltd and XYZ Ltd supply all the cement in a region, each selling 50 lakh tonnes a year at ₹6,000 a tonne. If ABC cuts its price by ₹300, XYZ matches and total demand does not change, each still sells 50 lakh tonnes but gives up ₹150 crore of revenue, which is why duopolists often avoid price wars.

short: A market dominated by a few large sellers, each big enough that its pricing and output decisions affect the others.
kid: If only three bakeries sell bread in your town, each keeps an eye on the others. When one changes the price of a loaf, the other two notice straight away.
detail: An oligopoly sits between perfect competition and monopoly: a handful of firms hold most of the market, usually because of high barriers to entry such as heavy capital needs, licences or scale economies. Because each firm's moves visibly affect rivals, strategy is interdependent; firms may fight on price, compete mainly on brand and features, or settle into stable pricing where nobody rocks the boat. Indian examples include cement, telecom, aviation, tyres and paints, where a few players control most capacity. Explicit coordination on prices or output is a cartel, which is illegal; the Competition Commission of India has imposed penalties on cement and tyre makers for alleged cartelisation. Concentration is measured by the top firms' combined share or the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index. A common confusion: oligopolies are not automatically cosy; airlines, for instance, often see brutal price competition.
example: Say four firms hold 40%, 30%, 20% and 10% of a market. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index is 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000, well above the 2,500 mark that the 2010 US merger guidelines treated as highly concentrated (the 2023 guidelines lowered that mark to 1,800).
formula: HHI = Sum of the squared market shares (in %) of all firms in the market

short: When a product becomes so similar across sellers that buyers choose mainly on price, squeezing every seller's profit margins.
kid: If every stall sells the same plain pencils, you just buy the cheapest one. The stalls then keep lowering their prices, so each one earns very little.
detail: Commoditisation is the process by which a once-differentiated product becomes interchangeable, so that brand, features and service no longer justify a price premium and competition shifts to price. It happens as technology spreads, patents expire, standards emerge and many suppliers enter; personal computers, basic phones, solar panels, generic medicines and many IT services have all faced it. A commodity business sells such undifferentiated output, like steel, cement, sugar or basic chemicals, where profits swing with the price cycle and the lowest-cost producer tends to win. For investors, commoditisation erodes pricing power and returns on capital, so companies fight it with branding, bundling, services and innovation. A common confusion is equating commoditisation with commodities traded on exchanges; it describes a competitive condition, not a type of asset.
example: Say ABC Ltd once sold a gadget at ₹5,000 that cost ₹3,000 to make, a 40% gross margin. After dozens of rivals copy it, the price falls to ₹3,300 while cost stays at ₹3,000, so the margin shrinks to about 9% (₹300 / ₹3,300).

short: The revenue and costs linked to a single unit of a business, such as one customer or one order, showing whether each unit makes money.
kid: If one cup of lemonade costs you three coins to make and you sell it for five, you keep two coins for every cup. Looking at one cup tells you if the stand works.
detail: Unit economics break a business down to its basic repeating unit, such as one customer, order, ride, store or subscription, and ask whether that unit is profitable on its own. Typical measures include contribution per order (revenue minus variable costs like delivery, payment fees and discounts), customer lifetime value against customer acquisition cost, and CAC payback period. Positive unit economics mean growth should eventually produce profit once fixed costs are covered; negative unit economics mean every extra sale deepens losses, so scaling up only makes things worse. After the 2022 funding slowdown, Indian startups in food delivery, quick commerce and edtech faced intense scrutiny of their unit economics. A common confusion is reading positive contribution per order as overall profitability; fixed costs such as technology, offices and head-office staff still have to be covered.
example: Say a delivery app earns ₹90 per order in commission and fees, and spends ₹50 on the rider, ₹10 on payment costs and ₹20 on discounts. Contribution per order is ₹90 - ₹80 = ₹10, so 10 lakh orders a month contribute ₹1 crore toward fixed costs.
formula: Contribution per unit = Revenue per unit - Variable costs per unit

short: The average amount a company spends on marketing and sales to win one new paying customer.
kid: If you give away sweets so new friends try your lemonade, count how many sweets it took to win each new buyer. That is what each new buyer cost you.
detail: Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is total sales and marketing spending in a period divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period. The spending should include advertising, promotions, discounts and cashbacks aimed at new users, referral bonuses, sales salaries and commissions, and agency fees. Blended CAC divides all spend by all new customers, including those who arrived on their own; paid CAC counts only customers from paid channels, so it is higher and more honest about marketing efficiency. CAC matters because growth only creates value if customers bring in more profit over their lifetime than it cost to win them, which is why it is paired with lifetime value. Many Indian consumer apps that relied on heavy cashbacks found their true CAC far higher than it first appeared. A common confusion is ignoring timing: spending this quarter may win customers next quarter.
example: Say ABC Ltd spends ₹2 crore on ads, ₹50 lakh on referral bonuses and ₹50 lakh on sales salaries in a quarter, and gains 20,000 new customers. Its CAC is ₹3 crore / 20,000 = ₹1,500 per customer.
formula: CAC = Total sales and marketing spend / Number of new customers acquired

short: The total profit a business expects to earn from one customer over the whole time that customer keeps buying from it.
kid: A friend who buys your lemonade every week for a whole year brings you far more coins than one who buys only once. Adding up all the coins from that friend shows what they are worth to you.
detail: Customer lifetime value, usually written LTV or CLV, estimates the total gross profit a customer generates from first purchase until they leave. A common simple version multiplies average revenue per customer per period by gross margin and divides by the churn rate per period, since 1 divided by churn approximates the expected customer lifetime. More careful models use cohort data, allow spending per customer to grow through upselling, and discount future cash flows. LTV matters because it caps how much a company can sensibly spend to win a customer, so it is almost always analysed alongside customer acquisition cost. A common confusion is computing LTV on revenue rather than gross profit, which overstates it badly. In lending and real estate, LTV usually means loan-to-value ratio, an entirely different measure, so read the context.
example: Say a subscriber pays ABC Ltd ₹500 a month, the gross margin is 80% and 4% of subscribers cancel each month. LTV is ₹500 × 0.8 / 0.04 = ₹10,000, since the average customer stays about 1 / 0.04 = 25 months.
formula: LTV = (Average revenue per customer per period × Gross margin) / Churn rate per period

short: A ratio comparing the profit a customer brings over their lifetime with the cost of winning them; above 1 means each customer pays back.
kid: If you give one sweet to win a new friend for your stand, and that friend later brings you three sweets, you made a good swap. Getting back more than you gave is the goal.
detail: The LTV to CAC ratio divides customer lifetime value by customer acquisition cost to test whether growth creates or destroys value. Below 1, the company loses money on every customer it wins; around 1, it merely breaks even on acquisition; a widely quoted rule of thumb, especially in software and subscription businesses, is that 3 or more signals healthy, efficient growth. A very high ratio, say above 5, can mean the company is under-investing in marketing and growing slower than it could. The ratio is only as good as its inputs: LTV must be based on gross profit and realistic churn, and CAC must include all acquisition spending. Investors pair it with CAC payback period, because a good ratio that takes years to realise still strains cash. A common confusion is quoting the ratio on revenue-based LTV, which flatters it.
example: Say ABC Ltd's customer lifetime value is ₹10,000 and its customer acquisition cost is ₹2,500. Its LTV to CAC ratio is ₹10,000 / ₹2,500 = 4, so each ₹1 spent winning customers brings back about ₹4 of lifetime gross profit.
formula: LTV to CAC ratio = Customer lifetime value / Customer acquisition cost

short: The number of months it takes for the gross profit from a new customer to repay what the company spent to acquire them.
kid: If it took six sweets to win a new customer for your stand, and they give you one sweet each week, you get all your sweets back after six weeks.
detail: CAC payback period measures how long a company takes to recover customer acquisition cost from the gross profit that customer generates. It is calculated as CAC divided by monthly revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin, giving a result in months. It is widely used in SaaS and subscription businesses, where payback of roughly 12 months or less is often treated as strong and 18 to 24 months as acceptable for large enterprise customers. Shorter payback means growth needs less outside funding, because cash spent on marketing comes back quickly and can be reinvested. Unlike the LTV to CAC ratio, payback does not depend on uncertain assumptions about how long customers stay, so many investors trust it more. A common confusion is using revenue instead of gross profit in the calculation, which makes payback look much faster than the cash reality.
example: Say ABC Ltd spends ₹6,000 to acquire a customer who pays ₹1,000 a month at a 75% gross margin. Monthly gross profit is ₹750, so CAC payback is ₹6,000 / ₹750 = 8 months.
formula: CAC payback period (months) = CAC / (Monthly revenue per customer × Gross margin)

short: The percentage of customers or subscribers who stop using or paying for a product during a given period.
kid: If ten friends come to your lemonade stand this month and two of them stop coming next month, you have lost some regulars. Keeping friends coming back matters a lot.
detail: Churn rate measures how quickly a business loses customers, usually as customers lost during a period divided by customers at the start of that period. Its complement, retention rate, is the share who stay. Telecom operators, streaming services, SaaS firms, insurers and brokers all track it closely. Because recurring-revenue businesses spend heavily to acquire customers, high churn is expensive: lost customers must be replaced just to stand still, and lifetime value falls. Small monthly differences compound sharply; 2% monthly churn loses about 22% of customers in a year, while 5% monthly loses about 46%. Analysts also track revenue churn, which captures downgrades as well as cancellations. A common confusion is mixing up monthly and annual churn, or dividing by a customer base swollen by new sign-ups during the period. In investing, churning means something else: excessive trading in a client's account.
example: Say ABC Ltd starts a month with 50,000 subscribers and 1,500 cancel during the month. Its monthly churn rate is 1,500 / 50,000 = 3%, and its retention rate is 97%.
formula: Churn rate = Customers lost during the period / Customers at the start of the period × 100; Retention rate = 100% - Churn rate

short: Tracking groups of customers who joined in the same period over time, to see how their retention and spending change.
kid: Think of all the kids who joined your club in June, and all who joined in July. Watching each group on its own shows which group keeps coming back.
detail: Cohort analysis groups users by a shared starting point, typically the month they signed up or first bought, and follows each group over later periods: how many are still active, how much they spend and how often they reorder. Results are usually shown as a triangular table with cohorts as rows and months since joining as columns. This reveals patterns that totals hide: a company's revenue can rise simply because it keeps adding new customers while each older cohort quietly fades. Healthy retention curves flatten after an early drop, and the best businesses show older cohorts spending more over time. Investors in Indian consumer internet and SaaS companies routinely ask for cohort data before backing them. A common confusion is comparing cohorts of different ages without lining them up by months since joining.
example: Say ABC Ltd's January cohort has 10,000 new users, of whom 4,000 are still active after three months. Its March cohort of 12,000 has 6,000 active after three months, so three-month retention improved from 40% to 50%.
formula: Cohort retention after n periods = Active users from the cohort in period n / Users in the cohort at the start × 100

short: Revenue a company expects to receive again and again, such as monthly subscriptions or yearly contracts, rather than from one-off sales.
kid: If a friend pays you one coin every week to bring lemonade to their door, you know those coins will keep coming. That is easier than hoping new people stop by.
detail: Recurring revenue is income that repeats on a predictable schedule under subscriptions, service contracts, memberships, maintenance agreements or usage-based plans. Examples include software subscriptions, streaming and mobile plans, annual maintenance contracts and asset-management fees. Because it is likely to continue, recurring revenue makes earnings more visible and less volatile, and investors usually value it more highly than one-time sales; that is a big reason subscription and SaaS companies often trade at high revenue multiples. Its quality depends on contract length, churn, pricing power and how concentrated the customers are. Indian IT services firms highlight annuity revenue from multi-year managed-service contracts for the same reason. A common confusion: recurring does not mean guaranteed, since customers can cancel, and repeat purchases without a contract, such as groceries, are usually called repeat rather than recurring revenue.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 2,000 business customers each paying ₹25,000 a month. Its recurring revenue is ₹5 crore a month, or ₹60 crore a year, before any new sales.

short: The yearly value of a company's active subscription contracts, a standard measure of size and growth for software and subscription businesses.
kid: Count the coins your friends pay each month for lemonade, then work out what that adds up to over a whole year if they all keep paying. That yearly total is it.
detail: Annual recurring revenue, or ARR, is the annualised value of recurring subscription contracts in force at a point in time. It is typically calculated as monthly recurring revenue multiplied by 12, or as the sum of annual contract values, and it excludes one-time items such as setup fees, consulting and hardware. ARR is the headline metric for SaaS companies and is closely watched by venture investors; Indian SaaS firms often announce funding rounds alongside ARR milestones, and an ARR of $100 million is widely treated as a scale threshold. Changes in ARR are broken into new, expansion, contraction and churned ARR. A common confusion is treating ARR as reported revenue: it is a run-rate snapshot, not an accounting figure defined by Ind AS or GAAP, so companies calculate it differently and some inflate it with uncontracted usage.
example: Say ABC Software has 400 customers on annual contracts averaging $30,000, plus $1 million of one-time implementation fees. Its ARR is 400 × $30,000 = $12 million; the implementation fees are excluded.
formula: ARR = MRR × 12 (or the sum of annualised values of active recurring contracts)

short: The predictable subscription revenue a business earns in a month, converted to a monthly figure and excluding one-time charges.
kid: If five friends each pay you one coin every month for lemonade, you know you will get five coins next month too. The coins you can count on each month are the number.
detail: Monthly recurring revenue, or MRR, is the total recurring subscription revenue a company expects each month from active customers, with annual or quarterly plans converted to a monthly amount. It excludes one-time fees, temporary discounts and usage that is not contracted. Early-stage SaaS and consumer subscription firms often track MRR more closely than ARR because it shows momentum month by month. MRR is broken into new MRR from new customers, expansion MRR from upgrades, contraction MRR from downgrades and churned MRR from cancellations; together these give net new MRR. A common confusion is booking an annual prepayment as one month's MRR: a ₹12,000 annual plan adds ₹1,000 of MRR, not ₹12,000. Like ARR, MRR is a management metric rather than an accounting revenue line, so definitions vary between companies.
example: Say ABC Ltd starts a month with ₹50 lakh of MRR, adds ₹6 lakh from new customers and ₹2 lakh from upgrades, and loses ₹3 lakh to cancellations. Ending MRR is ₹50 lakh + ₹6 lakh + ₹2 lakh - ₹3 lakh = ₹55 lakh, implying ARR of ₹6.6 crore.
formula: Net new MRR = New MRR + Expansion MRR - Contraction MRR - Churned MRR

short: Recurring revenue from existing customers today, as a percentage of what the same customers paid a year earlier, after upgrades, downgrades and cancellations.
kid: Last summer your friends bought ten cups of lemonade a week. This summer a few stopped, but others now buy more, so the same group buys twelve cups. Your old friends are buying more than before.
detail: Net revenue retention, also called net dollar retention, measures how recurring revenue from an existing customer base changes over a period, usually a year, ignoring revenue from new customers. Start with recurring revenue from customers at the beginning of the period, add expansion from upsells, cross-sells and price increases, subtract contraction from downgrades and churn from cancellations, then divide by the starting figure. Above 100% means the existing base grows on its own; leading SaaS companies have reported 120% or more, letting them grow before winning a single new customer. Below 100% means the company must keep acquiring customers just to stand still. Gross revenue retention, which ignores expansion and so cannot exceed 100%, shows how sticky the base is. A common confusion is mixing in revenue from customers who joined during the period, which inflates NRR.
example: Say ABC Software's existing customers paid $10 million of ARR a year ago. During the year they added $2.5 million through upgrades, cut $0.5 million through downgrades and cancelled $1 million. NRR is ($10m + $2.5m - $0.5m - $1m) / $10m = 110%.
formula: NRR = (Starting recurring revenue + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Starting recurring revenue × 100

short: The total value of goods sold through an online marketplace or platform in a period, before deducting discounts, returns, fees or cancellations.
kid: If children at a big school fair sell toys worth a hundred coins in all, that whole pile passed through the fair. The fair itself keeps only a small part for running it.
detail: Gross merchandise value, or GMV, is the total sales value of all orders transacted on a platform, such as an e-commerce marketplace, food-delivery or quick-commerce app, or travel site, over a period; food-delivery companies often call it gross order value. GMV is not the platform's revenue: on a marketplace, most of that money belongs to sellers, and the platform's revenue is its commissions, fees and advertising income, roughly GMV multiplied by the take rate. Companies also differ on whether GMV is counted before or after discounts, cancellations, returns, taxes and delivery charges, so figures are rarely comparable across firms. Indian e-commerce companies long led with GMV because it shows scale, but investors now focus more on net revenue, contribution margin and profit. A common confusion is valuing a marketplace on GMV as if it were revenue, which can overstate the business many times over.
example: Say a marketplace processes 50 lakh orders in a month with an average value of ₹800. Its GMV is ₹400 crore; if its take rate is 15%, its revenue from those orders is only ₹60 crore.
formula: GMV = Number of orders × Average order value

short: The share of the total value of transactions on a platform that the platform keeps as its own revenue.
kid: If you help friends sell their old toys and keep one coin out of every ten for your help, that one coin from each ten is your take.
detail: Take rate is a platform's revenue divided by the gross merchandise value or total payment volume that flows through it, expressed as a percentage. It captures commissions, payment and listing fees, delivery charges and often advertising income earned from sellers. Marketplaces, food-delivery apps, ride-hailing firms, app stores and payment companies are all analysed on it. Take rates vary widely, from low single digits for card payment processing to as much as 30% on some app-store sales. A rising take rate lifts revenue without more transactions, but pushing it too high invites sellers to leave, rivals to undercut and regulators to step in, as restaurant and app-developer complaints about commissions have shown in several countries, India included. A common confusion is comparing take rates across companies that define GMV differently or count items such as delivery fees inside or outside revenue.
example: Say a food-delivery app handles ₹1,000 crore of orders in a quarter and earns ₹200 crore from restaurant commissions, fees and ads. Its take rate is ₹200 crore / ₹1,000 crore = 20%.
formula: Take rate = Platform revenue / Gross merchandise value × 100

short: The average revenue a company earns from each user or subscriber in a period, usually a month.
kid: If your lemonade stand earns twenty coins in a week from ten friends, each friend brought in two coins on average. That tells you how much each friend spends.
detail: Average revenue per user, or ARPU, is total revenue from a service in a period divided by the average number of users or subscribers in that period. It is the key operating metric for Indian telecom operators, which report it every quarter and whose tariff hikes are judged by how much they lift ARPU; streaming, gaming, social-media and other digital businesses use it too. Because the user count at the start and end of a period differ, companies usually divide by the average subscriber base. Rising ARPU can come from price increases, users moving to richer plans, or a better customer mix. A common confusion is comparing ARPU across companies without checking definitions: some count only paying users (sometimes called ARPPU), some include free users, and telecom firms count each SIM rather than each person.
example: Say a telecom operator earns ₹6,000 crore of mobile revenue in a quarter and has 25 crore subscribers on average. Monthly ARPU is ₹6,000 crore / 25 crore / 3 months = ₹80.
formula: ARPU = Total revenue in the period / Average number of users in the period

short: The average amount a customer spends per order, found by dividing total sales by the number of orders.
kid: If three friends buy lemonade and together pay you nine coins, each one spent three coins on average. Shops are happy when that number goes up.
detail: Average order value, or AOV, is total revenue or order value in a period divided by the number of orders placed. It is a core metric for e-commerce, food-delivery, quick-commerce and retail businesses. AOV matters because many costs, such as delivery riders, packaging and payment processing, are incurred per order whatever its size, so a bigger basket spreads those costs and improves unit economics. Companies raise AOV through bundles, free-delivery thresholds, recommendations, nudges toward premium products and new categories; Indian quick-commerce apps have widened their ranges well beyond groceries partly to lift basket sizes. A common confusion is between AOV and revenue per customer: one customer may place many orders, so AOV says nothing about how often people buy. Analysts also check whether AOV growth reflects genuinely bigger baskets or simply inflation.
example: Say ABC Ltd's app processes 2 lakh orders worth ₹9 crore in a month, giving an AOV of ₹450. If delivery costs ₹45 an order, that is 10% of order value; lifting AOV to ₹600 cuts it to 7.5%.
formula: AOV = Total revenue (or order value) / Number of orders

short: The number of different people who use an app at least once in a month; daily active users measures the same per day.
kid: Count how many different friends come to play at your house this month. Even if one friend comes every single day, you count them just once.
detail: Monthly active users, or MAU, counts the unique users who performed a meaningful action in an app or online service during a month; daily active users, or DAU, does the same for a single day. They are the headline scale metrics for social networks, games, payment apps, streaming and other consumer internet businesses, and they feed into valuation through ARPU, since revenue roughly equals users multiplied by revenue per user. The DAU to MAU ratio, often called stickiness, shows how habitual a product is: a ratio of 50% means the average monthly user is active on about half the days. A common confusion is treating MAU as a standard figure: companies define active differently (opening the app, logging in or transacting), and downloads or registered users are much larger and far less meaningful numbers.
example: Say an app has 3 crore MAU and 90 lakh DAU on average. Its DAU to MAU ratio is 90 lakh / 3 crore = 30%, so a typical monthly user is active on about 9 days in a 30-day month.
formula: Stickiness = DAU / MAU × 100

short: How much a company's operating profit swings when its sales change, which depends on how much of its costs are fixed.
kid: Your lemonade stand must pay for its table whether you sell one cup or a hundred. Once the table is paid for, every extra cup adds lots of coins, but slow days hurt more.
detail: Operating leverage arises when a large share of a company's costs are fixed, such as rent, salaries, depreciation and technology, rather than varying with each unit sold. Once sales cover fixed costs, much of each extra rupee of revenue drops to operating profit, so profits grow faster than sales; the same structure magnifies losses when sales fall. The degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures this as the percentage change in EBIT for a 1% change in sales, or equivalently contribution divided by EBIT. Airlines, telecom, software, hotels and cement plants have high operating leverage, which is why their earnings can jump sharply in an upcycle. Indian analysts often say operating leverage is kicking in when a fast-growing company's margins expand. A common confusion is with financial leverage, which comes from fixed interest costs on debt rather than fixed operating costs.
example: Say ABC Ltd has sales of ₹100 crore, variable costs of ₹40 crore and fixed costs of ₹40 crore, giving EBIT of ₹20 crore. Its DOL is ₹60 crore contribution / ₹20 crore EBIT = 3, so a 10% rise in sales to ₹110 crore lifts EBIT by 30% to ₹26 crore.
formula: DOL = % change in EBIT / % change in sales = Contribution / EBIT

short: A company's plan and timeline for moving from losses to lasting profits, usually by growing revenue, improving margins and cutting costs.
kid: If your lemonade stand spends more coins than it earns, you make a plan: sell more cups, waste fewer lemons and spend less on signs. Following that plan helps you keep coins at last.
detail: Path to profitability describes how a loss-making company, typically a startup or newly listed tech firm, expects to reach consistent profits, and roughly when. A credible path rests on specific levers: positive and improving unit economics, operating leverage as fixed costs are spread over more revenue, higher take rates or prices, lower customer acquisition costs and reduced cash burn. Investors track milestones such as positive contribution margin, adjusted EBITDA breakeven, then net profit and free cash flow. After the 2022 funding slowdown, Indian startups and newly listed tech companies came under pressure to show a clear path, and many cut discounts, staff and marketing to get there. A common confusion is treating adjusted EBITDA breakeven as profitability; it usually excludes employee stock option costs, depreciation and interest, so net profit can still be negative.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹30 of contribution per order and has fixed costs of ₹60 crore a quarter, so it breaks even at ₹60 crore / ₹30 = 2 crore orders a quarter. At 1.5 crore orders today and 10% growth per quarter, it crosses that level in the fourth quarter from now, when orders reach about 1.5 crore × 1.1^4 = 2.2 crore.
formula: Break-even volume = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit

short: Software that customers use over the internet for a regular subscription fee, instead of buying it once and installing it on their own computers.
kid: Instead of buying a whole bike, you pay a little each month to ride one whenever you like. Some computer programs work like that: you pay to use them, not to own them.
detail: Software as a service, or SaaS, is a delivery and business model in which the vendor runs software in the cloud and customers use it through a browser or app, paying a subscription, usually per user or by usage, instead of a large upfront licence. The vendor handles hosting, updates and security. Email and office suites, customer-relationship management, accounting and HR software are common examples. Investors like SaaS because of recurring revenue, high gross margins (often 70% to 80% or more at scale) and expansion within existing customers, and they analyse it with ARR, net revenue retention, churn, CAC payback and the Rule of 40. India has built a sizeable SaaS industry selling largely to global customers, including firms such as Freshworks and Zoho. A common confusion: SaaS describes how software is sold and delivered, not what it does; heavy early losses while acquiring customers are normal.
example: Say ABC Cloud charges $50 per user per month and a client with 200 users signs an annual plan. The client pays $50 × 200 × 12 = $120,000 a year, adding $10,000 of MRR, or $120,000 of ARR, for ABC.

short: A business model in which customers pay a regular fee, monthly or yearly, for continued access to a product or service.
kid: Instead of buying a comic book each time, your family pays a little every month and a new comic arrives at your door. It keeps coming as long as you keep paying.
detail: In a subscription model, customers pay recurring fees for ongoing access rather than making one-time purchases. It spans streaming and news, software, mobile plans, gyms, meal kits, cloud storage and even cars and appliances on rental plans. For the company, subscriptions create predictable recurring revenue, richer customer data and a direct relationship that supports upselling, and investors often value subscription revenue at a premium for that predictability. The economics depend on acquiring customers at a reasonable cost and keeping them, so churn, customer lifetime value, CAC payback and pricing tiers are the key metrics. Many streaming platforms in India pair paid plans with low-priced mobile-only tiers suited to price-sensitive users. A common confusion is assuming any subscription business is profitable; heavy discounts to win sign-ups and high churn can make it lose money on every customer.
example: Say a streaming service has 10 lakh subscribers paying ₹149 a month. That is ₹14.9 crore of monthly recurring revenue; if 5% cancel in a month and none are replaced, 9.5 lakh subscribers remain, bringing in ₹14.155 crore.
